title: Gibbs Energies and Phase Diagrams
lead: How the Gibbs energy behaves across a phase change classifies the transition by order. The slopes of G against temperature and pressure give the entropies and molar volumes of the phases, and other forms of work add their own pairs of variables to G.

exercises.source_id: This classification goes back to Ehrenfest.
exercises.prompt: At a transition temperature, the Gibbs energy of a material is smooth, its entropy is continuous but changes slope, and its heat capacity $\kCP$ jumps from one finite value to another. In the Ehrenfest classification, what order is the transition?

answer.hint: Find the lowest derivative of G that is discontinuous.
answer.solution: The order is the order of the first derivative of $\kG$ to go discontinuous. $\kG$ itself and its first derivatives, $\kSent$ and $\kHenth$, are continuous (the entropy only has a kink), and the first discontinuity is the jump in the second derivative $\kCP$. That is the second-order row of Table 23.2.1. In a first-order transition such as melting, $\kG$ would have a kink, $\kSent$ would jump and $\kCP$ would go to infinity.

footnotes.html: In the second-order column of the sketch, the $C_P$ panel labels its two curves solid and liquid. They are the ordered and disordered phases, as in the $G$ and $S$ panels above it.
Above the critical temperature there is one fluid phase, and Figure 13.7(d) draws its $\kGbar(\kP)$ as a single smooth curve. The line shows no derivative discontinuity there.
